title: Optimize N+1 Query in Order History API

hints.title: Where to look
hints.body: Find the `GET /orders` route handler. It fetches a list of orders, then look at what happens inside the loop that follows. Count how many database calls are made for a user with N orders — you should see a pattern that grows linearly with N.

hints.title: The concept
hints.body: This is the **N+1 query problem**. The handler makes 1 query to get the list of orders, then makes 1 additional query *per order* to fetch its line items — so N orders = N+1 total database round-trips. With 50 orders that's 51 queries for a single API call. The fix is to replace the per-order lookup with a single **batch query** that fetches all items for all orders at once.

hints.title: The fix approach
hints.body:
Replace the `for...of` loop that calls `db.getOrderItems(order.id)` with a single call to `db.getOrderItemsBatch(orderIds)`. The steps are:
1. Collect all order IDs into an array: `const orderIds = orders.map(o => o.id)`.
2. Call `const itemsMap = await db.getOrderItemsBatch(orderIds)` — this returns a `{ [orderId]: items[] }` map in 1 query.
3. Build the response by mapping over `orders` and looking up `itemsMap[order.id]`.

Result: 2 queries total (1 for orders + 1 batch for items), regardless of how many orders the user has.

badPatches.title: In-Memory Request Caching
badPatches.summary: 80/100 — passes visible tests (60/60) and H2, fails H1 (O(1) query count on first request)
